lead: Both readings today are about the time in between: the time after the Lord has gone to the Father and before he returns. Paul tells the Corinthians how to live it when the body grows weak: “we do not lose heart”, because something within is being renewed day by day. In Luke the nobleman goes away to receive royal power and leaves his servants with one pound each and a single command: “Do business with these until I come back.” The key words are renewal and faithfulness.

set: Paul wrote 2 Corinthians from Macedonia, probably around AD 55–57, in a hard season of his ministry. In chapter 4 he speaks of the Gospel as a treasure carried “in clay jars” (4:7), and of himself as “afflicted in every way, but not crushed” (4:8). Just before our verses he gives the ground of his hope: the one who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also (4:14). Today's three verses draw the conclusion.
str: v. 16: we do not lose heart: the outer nature wastes away, the inner nature is renewed.
v. 17: light and passing affliction set beside an eternal weight of glory.
v. 18: what is seen and passes, and what is unseen and lasts.
kw: The same words open the chapter (4:1). To lose heart is to give up in weariness. Paul does not say he never feels tired. He says he does not give in to it.

Literally “the outer person” and “the inner person”. Paul is not dividing body from soul as if the body did not matter. The outer person is our life as it can be seen and as it ages; the inner person is the life that God is making new in us.
In Hebrew the word for glory, kābôd, also carries the sense of weight. Paul puts the two on a scale: the affliction is light, the glory is heavy.
vv: Even though our outer nature is wasting away, our inner nature is being renewed day by day.
“Day by day” is the rhythm of grace. Renewal is not only a single event at Baptism. It goes on in every day that is lived with Christ, even in old age and sickness.
For this slight momentary affliction is preparing us for an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure,

Paul had been beaten, shipwrecked and imprisoned (11:23–27). He calls it “slight” and “momentary” only because he has set it beside eternity. In Romans he says the same: the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed (Romans 8:18).
because we look not at what can be seen but at what cannot be seen;
The verb means to keep one's eyes fixed on a goal, as a runner looks at the finish.
ch: The Church hears in these verses the virtue of hope, by which we desire eternal life as our happiness and rely not on our own strength but on the grace of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1817). They are often read at funerals and in the care of the sick, because they say what faith sees when the body fails. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this letter, says that Paul makes affliction light by setting it beside the reward, and short by setting it beside eternity (Homilies on 2 Corinthians, in substance).

r.h: Do business with these until I come back
set: Jesus is now near Jerusalem. He has just stayed in the house of Zacchaeus at Jericho (19:1–10), and the next scene is his entry into the city (19:28–40). Luke says why he tells this parable: the crowd “supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately” (19:11). The parable answers that there will be a time of absence first, and a time of work.

The story would have sounded familiar. When Herod the Great died in 4 BC, his son Archelaus went to Rome to have his kingship confirmed by the emperor, and a delegation followed him to oppose it (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 17). Jesus uses this kind of event as the frame of his story. Matthew has a similar parable with talents (Matthew 25:14–30), but in Luke every servant receives the same sum: one mina, about a hundred days' wages.
str: v. 11: why the parable is told.
vv. 12–14: the nobleman leaves; ten servants receive a pound each; the citizens refuse him.
vv. 15–19: he returns as king; two servants are rewarded with cities.
vv. 20–26: the third servant, who hid the pound out of fear.
v. 27: judgment on those who refused his rule.
kw: A Greek sum of money worth a hundred drachmas. It is not a fortune. The servants are tested on something modest, so that faithfulness, not natural ability, is what counts.
To trade, to put to work. The gift is not given to be kept safe but to be used and to grow.
The master's praise is not “successful” but “trustworthy”. The same word is used of the faithful steward in 12:42 and of being faithful in a very little in 16:10.
vv: Do business with these until I come back.

These words describe the life of the Church between the Ascension and the Lord's return. Luke opens Acts with the same horizon: “This Jesus… will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11).
Well done, good slave! Because you have been trustworthy in a very small thing, take charge of ten cities.
The reward is far beyond the work. A single pound becomes authority over ten cities. God is never outdone in generosity.
for I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man;
The third servant does nothing wrong with the money; he simply does nothing. What paralyses him is a false picture of his master. He is judged “by your own words” (19:22).
I tell you, to all those who have, more will be given;
A law of the spiritual life: grace used grows, grace buried withers.
ch: Many interpreters see in the one pound the gift that every Christian receives alike, such as the word of God and the grace of Baptism, and in the cities the share in Christ's reign that he gives to the faithful. The harsh last verse belongs to the world of the story, where kings punished rebels. It is a warning that to refuse Christ's kingship has consequences, not a picture of a cruel Jesus: in the very next scene he weeps over Jerusalem (19:41). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church is a pilgrim, already sharing in the last age, who waits for the Lord's return and works while she waits (Lumen Gentium 48).

qa: Is God really a harsh master who reaps where he did not sow?

No. Those are the frightened servant's words, not the truth about the master, who in fact gives cities for a pound. The parable shows how fear can freeze a believer. St John writes: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). We work for the Lord not as slaves who dread him but as children who trust him.
rite: The Panchangam remembers today St Sophia, without saying which of the holy women of that name is meant. The name itself is a word to pray with: sophia is Greek for wisdom. Today's readings show what that wisdom is: to weigh things by eternity, and to use faithfully, while we wait, what the Lord has entrusted to us.
study: What is the “one pound” the Lord has given me, and am I trading with it or keeping it wrapped in a cloth?
Paul's outer nature was wasting away. Where do I see my own inner nature being renewed day by day, and how can the Holy Qurbono feed that renewal?
